title: Introduction to std::string
recap: std::string, provided by the <string> header, owns its character data. A mutable std::string can be initialized, assigned text of a different length, and appended to without manually managing storage.

The length() member function reports the number of char elements and excludes the null terminator. Restricting this deterministic exercise to ASCII makes the reported character count unambiguous because every displayed character occupies one char element.
objectives: Replace its initial contents using assignment.
Report a deterministic ASCII string length with length().
warnings: A const std::string cannot be reassigned or appended to.
std::string::length() counts char elements, not user-perceived Unicode characters.
Do not hard-code the final string or its length in the output expression.
challenge: Repair the mutable owned label so it is first reassigned from C++ to C++ Lab and then appended with a space and 2026. Print the resulting label and obtain its deterministic ASCII length by calling label.length().
hints: The label must own its text and change after initialization, so it should be a non-const std::string.
Assignment replaces the old contents: use label = "C++ Lab" for the first change.
Use label += " 2026" to append, then stream label.length() rather than the number 12.
